title: Live updates: 2026 US midterm elections and results
excerpt: Vice-President JD Vance also cites the war as the reason for his party's defeat.

1. Who is the Democrats' Mississippi hopeful Scott Colom?published at 04:47 GMT

    Ana Faguy
    Reporting from Washington DC

    All eyes are on Mississippi right now, where just over 1,100 votes separate Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, and Scott Colom, her Democratic challenger - who are vying to represent their state in the Senate.

    While we wait for all the ballots to be counted - and it could take a little while - here's what you need to know about Colom:

    • He currently works as a District Attorney and previously was a prosecutor and judge
    • President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a federal judge in the Northern District of Mississippi but his nomination was blocked in the US Senate by Hyde-Smith
    • While the Mississippi Senate race was not on the radar for many Americans, some big name Democrats appeared to see the potential victory in recent weeks, with former President Bill Clinton, former Vice-President Kamala Harris and Georgia Senator Raphael Warnock all campaigning on his behalf
    • When Hyde-Smith dismissed Mississippians' frustrations about high beef prices and suggested residents of her state "pick another protein", Colom took the remarks and ran, turning them into a television advert telling Mississippians to "pick another Senator" - which gained traction nationally
    • If Colom wins, he’ll be the first Mississippi Democrat elected to the US Senate in nearly 40 years and he will be the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction
    • Colom is a seventh-generation Mississippian and father of two.

  2. Midterm results a 'victory' for Canadians hopeful of tariff reliefpublished at 04:18 GMT

    Nadine Yousif
    Senior Canada reporter

    It was the midterm result that many in Canada had hoped for - a Democratic sweep that was in part a repudiation by American voters of Donald Trump's tariffs on close trade allies.

    "I was doing cartwheels down the street," said Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Wednesday morning, calling it "a victory for Canada".

    Tuesday night's result is unlikely to grant Canada relief from those tariffs any time soon, but there is anticipation that the political shifts could create a more favourable environment for Ottawa to get the best deal now that trade talks are back on.

    Democratic leaders like Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, now newly empowered, have both pushed to rein in the tariffs on Canada in recent months.

    Still, Democratic control of Congress might not do much to move the needle on tariffs. Trump's levies have been largely enacted using executive orders without approval from Congress.

  3. Democrats' sweeping election win leaves Alaska as 'nice to have'published at 03:55 GMT

    We're still waiting on the results of Alaska's Senate race, where Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan by some 600 votes.

    But following the Democrats' resounding result on election night, the race that they were determined to win has become a "nice to have", reports North America correspondent Shaimaa Khalil.

  4. Finger pointing has begun inside the Republican Partypublished at 03:31 GMT

    Will Grant
    BBC correspondent

    After its most bruising night in more than 30 years, the introspection – and finger pointing – have begun inside the Republican Party

    Voters across the country had made it clear their ballots would be a reckoning for Trump's decision to go to war with Iran.

    Now some of his closest allies are distancing themselves from the conflict, most noticeably Vice-President JD Vance.

    "The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on social media. "And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

    It was a point which Trump begrudgingly accepted as he spoke to journalists at the construction site of a new ballroom at the White House.

    But he insisted he still would not have done anything differently. "You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.

    Many interpret the vice-president's comments as an unofficial launch of his own presidential bid in 2028.

    The results are also being seen as a sign that the US is witnessing the beginning of the end of the MAGA movement under Trump.

  5. 'Texas is blue - that is a hard sentence to utter', says Senator Ted Cruzpublished at 03:08 GMT

    Republican Texas Senator Ted Cruz says the midterm results amount not just to a "blue wave", but a "blue tsunami".

    "Nowhere are the consequences of this election greater than Texas," he writes on social media, after the state elected a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in decades in 37-year-old James Talarico.

    Democrat Gina Hinojosa also ousted Greg Abbott, one of the nation's most high-profile Republican governors.

    Pointing to the cost of living and poverty, Cruz says there was "very real pain from real Americans, and too many Republican politicians seem like they didn't understand or they didn't care".

    "Texas is blue. That is a hard sentence to utter," he writes, and says the Republicans need to rebuild as a "true blue-collar party" after losing core support among rural communities, Hispanic voters and young people.

  6. Republicans bent the rules to beat this Democrat. He still wonpublished at 02:34 GMT

    Brandon Drenon
    US reporter

    Democrat Shomari Figures won re-election to Congress in Alabama, despite having to run in a district that Republican state lawmakers specifically designed to defeat him.

    "We never felt that we were an underdog in this race," Figures told the BBC, after his victory in a district that Trump won in 2024 by double digits.

    The Alabama Democrat was one of several candidates targeted this election in a process called redistricting – or gerrymandering – where lines on voting maps are redrawn, often to favour one party.

    Both Democrats and Republicans employed the tactic this election cycle, but Republicans led the way, heeding a direct request from Trump.

    But the move backfired.

    Texas, which redistricted five congressional seats to Republicans' advantage, lost four of those seats to Democrats, and Florida Republicans are on track to lose all four seats they redrew.

    Asked about Democrats' sweeping victories, Figures said: "I think people are just tired, man. They're tired of the overall economy. They're tired of being lied to. They're tired of the country kind of being run like it’s a reality show."

  7. Why is the Senate race so close in Republican stronghold Mississippi?published at 02:09 GMT

    Just hundreds of votes separate the candidates in Mississippi's Senate race, which has become an unlikely battleground in traditionally Republican territory.

    The BBC's Carl Nasman looks at how we got here and when the results might be called.

  8. Voter backlash to AI data centres a surprise, says OpenAI presidentpublished at 01:53 GMT

    Lily Jamali
    North America Technology Correspondent

    OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman has said he was caught off guard by the backlash to data centres in these elections.

    "I don't think anyone could say they were not surprised by that," Brockman said while speaking at the WSJ Tech conference in California on Wednesday.

    "It is definitely an issue that's very singular. No-one's ever seen something like that in American politics."

    "A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that, from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can’t just tweet and say, like, 'this is going to be good'.

    "You need to be in those communities," Brockman continued.

    "We need to do a better job of really communicating to people, to local communities, about why data centres can be beneficial to them."

  9. Democrats extend narrow lead in Mississippi Senate racepublished at 01:32 GMT

    Mississippi's Senate race remains on a knife-edge with some 96% of the votes counted.

    The latest tally shows Democratic candidate Scott Colom leading by a margin of 1,138, - about 0.1% of the total votes - as of about an hour ago.

    An hour before that, his lead on Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith was just 65 votes.

  10. How the Hispanic vote changed the course of the Texas electionpublished at 00:56 GMT

    Gary O'Donoghue
    Chief North America correspondent in Austin, Texas

    I first met Mario Guerrero, a businessman who lives in South Texas near the Mexican border, a few weeks ago. He has voted for President Donald Trump three times.

    The main issues on his mind during those elections? Immigration and border security.

    But years later, those same issues have driven him to flip his ballot. He voted Democrat in yesterday's midterm election, which sent Texas Democrats to the US Senate and governor's office for the first time in decades.

    Guerrero tells me today he doesn't necessarily identify with either party, and Democrats will still have to prove themselves.

    "I don't think that anybody gets a free pass here. Just because they (Democrats) won doesn't mean that it's all sunshine and rainbows. There's work we have to do," he says.

    But "the immigration enforcement has been something that's been mishandled by the current administration," he tells me.

    And he's not alone.

    Hispanic voters in Texas have voted for Democrat James Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton by two to one, according to voter poll data.

    This group previously backed Donald Trump in the 2024 Presidential election. Now many say the "cruelty" of US immigration enforcement has pushed them away from the Republican Party.

    Read more here on how the tide change in the state began.

  11. Expensive Republican campaigns did not pay off in some Senate racespublished at 00:29 GMT

    Jake Horton
    BBC News

    This year’s midterms campaign is set to be the most expensive ever - with most of that money being spent on advertising.

    The top five Senate races for ad spending were in the battleground states of Ohio, Texas, Michigan, Iowa and Maine, as of the end of October according to advert tracking firm AdImpact, external.

    The Republican candidates are projected to lose every one of those. That's despite spending more than $280m (£207m) more than their Democratic opponents across the five contests.

    In total, the Republican campaigns spent about $960m (£713m) on advertising in those unsuccessful Senate races.

    The biggest spending gap was in Texas - where Democratic candidate James Talarico was outspent by more than $140m (£103m) by Republican candidate Ken Paxton on ads.

    Talarico is set to win that race by more than 10 percentage points.

    The only contest in which the Republican was outspent was in Iowa - where Democratic candidate Josh Turek is set to win by about five points.

  12. Mail-in ballots being counted by hand in some close-call racespublished at 00:12 GMT

    Though we know the overall results of the midterm elections already, there are a few races that are still too close to call.

    In states like Mississippi, where the Senate race had come down to a razor-thin margin of votes, it could take a week to know who won as mail-in ballots continue to arrive.

    In some places, these ballots are hand counted.

    In Los Angeles, California, officials are still counting ballots to determine who will be the next mayor. Take a look:

  13. Democrat candidate 1,138 votes ahead in razor thin Mississippi racepublished at 00:04 GMT

    A little bit ago, we told you that more votes were not expected to be tallied in the Mississippi Senate race today, according to Mississippi's Democratic Party chairman.

    But we've just had more numbers in, showing that Democratic candidate Scott Colom has widened his lead.

    He is now ahead by 1,138 votes, according to data from the Associated Press.

    Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, has 48.9% of the vote. Colom has 49%. Counting is ongoing.

  14. Market perception crystalises post-election - it will have a real-world impactpublished at 23:57 GMT 4 November

    Faisal Islam
    Economics editor

    At first markets did not quite know how to react to the Democrats' "blue wave". The significant market reaction crystallised after Vice-President JD Vance’s remarkable social media message suggested lost voters wanted to "end the war".

    Crude oil markets had been factoring in a chance of a significant escalation in the Iran war in the coming days and weeks, pushing up the oil price close to $117 (£86.82) late last week.

    Today saw a significant 8-9% on-the-day fall in Brent crude to below $95 (£70.49) a barrel. It showed market belief that the manner of the Democrat sweep would serve to restrain the president.

    Trump still has the formal power to decide on military action, but this was an historic electoral loss directly driven by cost-of-living pressure, in turn inextricably linked to his war choices.

    The markets may be wrong or right, but even this market perception will have a real-world impact. Already European gas prices, and US fuel prices have also fallen back.

    It is worth remembering that in the UK an expected increase in interest rates tomorrow has been explicitly linked to expectations of higher inflation from a longer Gulf War.

    It is a reminder that the rest of the world is waiting on the president.

  15. In his message to voters, Vance is also making a pitch for 2028published at 23:36 GMT 4 November

    Tom Bateman
    Reporting from Columbus, Ohio

    Vance is telling Republicans not to get angry at the defeat but to win the argument.

    His lengthy post is saying his party lost because it abandoned its basic promise to voters in 2024 to bring down prices and avoid foreign wars. But the movement has also been at odds with itself over all this for the last year or so.

    A row broke out among MAGA Republicans, involving some of the movement’s key influencers, over support for Trump’s policies on the Iran war and US backing for Israel.

    Vance opposed the war. He’s implying those, like Tucker Carlson, who implied it would tank Trump’s presidency are being proved right. His rallying cry distances him from the president and tries to burnish his credentials for “America First” retrenchment.

    Make no mistake, this is the start of his pitch as battle begins for the succession to Trump. But it will have to play with a wounded president still stuck by the ongoing crisis he created in the Middle East, a stalemated war with Iran.

  17. Mississippi Senate race won't be decided for days, state Democrat tells BBCpublished at 22:57 GMT 4 November

    Breaking

    Adam Moyer
    Reporting from Jackson, Mississippi

    More votes are not expected to be tallied in the state today, Mississippi Democratic Party Chair Cheikh Taylor tells the BBC.

    "On good intel it's my understanding that the election won't be decided until Monday," he says of the close Senate race here.

  18. Just 65 votes separates candidates in Mississippi's senate racepublished at 22:56 GMT 4 November

    This is where the current race in Mississippi sits right now.

    Democratic candidate Scott Colom is slightly ahead in the race to unseat incumbent Senator Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith.

    Colom, with 462,857 votes, at the time of writing, is ahead by 65 votes between him and Hyde‑Smith's 462,792 votes.

    Independent candidate Ty Pinkins has almost 20,000 votes.

    The race is too close to call after almost 96% of the votes counted.

    Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson says in a statement that 70 of the 82 counties in the state have uploaded their unofficial result through a state system, and notes that counties get 10 days from election day to submit their certified results to his office.

    There are some 3,600 outstanding absentee-by-mail ballots yet to be received and an unknown number of affidavit ballots to be processed in that 10-day timeframe, he says.

  19. Few people had Mississippi Senate race on their radar - now it's a close contestpublished at 22:42 GMT 4 November

    Carl Nasman
    Reporting from Jackson, Mississippi

    We're literally talking about a handful of ballots separating the two Senate candidates here in Mississippi.

    Scott Colom has a very small lead - fewer than 100 votes - over the Republican incumbant Cindy Hyde-Smith.

    If you looked back a few weeks ago, very few people had Mississippi on their radar, but Colom has run a grassroots campaign here.

    In this election we've seen candidates like Hyde-Smith - who are aligned with President Trump - underperform.

    This is another example of that - Democrats have had a strong showing in Republican strongholds.

  20. How long until we know the results in Mississippi?published at 22:18 GMT 4 November

    Brandon Drenon
    US reporter

    We are still waiting to hear results for the Mississippi Senate race, and it could be a while before we know the winner in the race between Democrat Scott Colom and incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

    Mississippi does not have automatic recounts for tight races or allow candidates to request recounts.

    The state also allows mail-in ballots to be counted if they are postmarked by election day and received within five business days later.

    That means the race is very likely not to be called until at least 10 November, says Julie Wronski, an associate professor of political science at the University of Mississippi.

    "Because the difference between the two candidates is so narrow, really, we're going to have to wait for every single vote received in any capacity to be counted," Wronski says.

    The vote spread between the two candidates is currently less than 100 ballots, according to data from the Associated Press.

    After its most bruising night in more than 30 years, the introspection – and finger pointing – have begun inside the Republican Party

    Voters across the country had made it clear their ballots would be a reckoning for Trump's decision to go to war with Iran.

    Now some of his closest allies are distancing themselves from the conflict, most noticeably Vice-President JD Vance.

    "The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on social media. "And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

    It was a point which Trump begrudgingly accepted as he spoke to journalists at the construction site of a new ballroom at the White House.

    But he insisted he still would not have done anything differently. "You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.

    Many interpret the vice-president's comments as an unofficial launch of his own presidential bid in 2028.

    The results are also being seen as a sign that the US is witnessing the beginning of the end of the MAGA movement under Trump.

    Brandon Drenon
    US reporter

    Democrat Shomari Figures won re-election to Congress in Alabama, despite having to run in a district that Republican state lawmakers specifically designed to defeat him.

    "We never felt that we were an underdog in this race," Figures told the BBC, after his victory in a district that Trump won in 2024 by double digits.

    The Alabama Democrat was one of several candidates targeted this election in a process called redistricting – or gerrymandering – where lines on voting maps are redrawn, often to favour one party.

    Both Democrats and Republicans employed the tactic this election cycle, but Republicans led the way, heeding a direct request from Trump.

    But the move backfired.

    Texas, which redistricted five congressional seats to Republicans' advantage, lost four of those seats to Democrats, and Florida Republicans are on track to lose all four seats they redrew.

    Asked about Democrats' sweeping victories, Figures said: "I think people are just tired, man. They're tired of the overall economy. They're tired of being lied to. They're tired of the country kind of being run like it’s a reality show."

    Gary O'Donoghue
    Chief North America correspondent in Austin, Texas

    I first met Mario Guerrero, a businessman who lives in South Texas near the Mexican border, a few weeks ago. He has voted for President Donald Trump three times.

    The main issues on his mind during those elections? Immigration and border security.

    But years later, those same issues have driven him to flip his ballot. He voted Democrat in yesterday's midterm election, which sent Texas Democrats to the US Senate and governor's office for the first time in decades.

    Guerrero tells me today he doesn't necessarily identify with either party, and Democrats will still have to prove themselves.

    "I don't think that anybody gets a free pass here. Just because they (Democrats) won doesn't mean that it's all sunshine and rainbows. There's work we have to do," he says.

    But "the immigration enforcement has been something that's been mishandled by the current administration," he tells me.

    And he's not alone.

    Hispanic voters in Texas have voted for Democrat James Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton by two to one, according to voter poll data.

    This group previously backed Donald Trump in the 2024 Presidential election. Now many say the "cruelty" of US immigration enforcement has pushed them away from the Republican Party.

    Read more here on how the tide change in the state began.

    Jake Horton
    BBC News

    This year’s midterms campaign is set to be the most expensive ever - with most of that money being spent on advertising.

    The top five Senate races for ad spending were in the battleground states of Ohio, Texas, Michigan, Iowa and Maine, as of the end of October according to advert tracking firm AdImpact, external.

    The Republican candidates are projected to lose every one of those. That's despite spending more than $280m (£207m) more than their Democratic opponents across the five contests.

    In total, the Republican campaigns spent about $960m (£713m) on advertising in those unsuccessful Senate races.

    The biggest spending gap was in Texas - where Democratic candidate James Talarico was outspent by more than $140m (£103m) by Republican candidate Ken Paxton on ads.

    Talarico is set to win that race by more than 10 percentage points.

    The only contest in which the Republican was outspent was in Iowa - where Democratic candidate Josh Turek is set to win by about five points.

• Market perception crystalises post-election - it will have a real-world impactpublished at 23:57 GMT 4 November

    Faisal Islam
    Economics editor

    At first markets did not quite know how to react to the Democrats' "blue wave". The significant market reaction crystallised after Vice-President JD Vance’s remarkable social media message suggested lost voters wanted to "end the war".

    Crude oil markets had been factoring in a chance of a significant escalation in the Iran war in the coming days and weeks, pushing up the oil price close to $117 (£86.82) late last week.

    Today saw a significant 8-9% on-the-day fall in Brent crude to below $95 (£70.49) a barrel. It showed market belief that the manner of the Democrat sweep would serve to restrain the president.

    Trump still has the formal power to decide on military action, but this was an historic electoral loss directly driven by cost-of-living pressure, in turn inextricably linked to his war choices.

    The markets may be wrong or right, but even this market perception will have a real-world impact. Already European gas prices, and US fuel prices have also fallen back.

    It is worth remembering that in the UK an expected increase in interest rates tomorrow has been explicitly linked to expectations of higher inflation from a longer Gulf War.

    It is a reminder that the rest of the world is waiting on the president.

• How long until we know the results in Mississippi?published at 22:18 GMT 4 November

    Brandon Drenon
    US reporter

    We are still waiting to hear results for the Mississippi Senate race, and it could be a while before we know the winner in the race between Democrat Scott Colom and incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

    Mississippi does not have automatic recounts for tight races or allow candidates to request recounts.

    The state also allows mail-in ballots to be counted if they are postmarked by election day and received within five business days later.

    That means the race is very likely not to be called until at least 10 November, says Julie Wronski, an associate professor of political science at the University of Mississippi.

    "Because the difference between the two candidates is so narrow, really, we're going to have to wait for every single vote received in any capacity to be counted," Wronski says.

    The vote spread between the two candidates is currently less than 100 ballots, according to data from the Associated Press.
